utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. And good morning to everybody out there in New York. [Microphone not activated]... Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, can we have appearances for starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, Lorna Bolton, Carmela Javier, and Mark Harmon for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Daniela Tasic, Chad Mair, Colleen Rohan, Katharine Marshall, Tina Drolec, Milos Androvic, Novak Lukic, and I'm Guy-Smith on behalf of General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Good afternoon to you, Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good morning, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning. I beg your pardon. I've been up for a long time. Mr. Sacirbey, the ritual again, you are bounds by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I understand, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Guy-Smith, before I call you, simply because of the urgency of the matter and the lack of time, the Chamber has now received the response from the Prosecution yesterday. And we'll just give an oral ruling to grant the alternative of the application.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are welcome. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I trust you had a good sleep.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could have used a little more, but otherwise, it's been quite good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to start today's discussion with a quote, and I think we'll move from that position, and I'm going to be dealing with the issue of diplomacy. Ambrose Bierce said, Diplomacy is it the patriotic art of lying for one's country. And I don't believe that he said that in a necessarily negative fashion but, rather, a recognition of what indeed occurred in the world of the, what I'll call for the moment, real politik and diplomacy. You've told us that you were an ambassador, and I believe it would be fair to say that you, for some period of time of your life, were a diplomat; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you, Mr. Guy-Smith. I'm awfully sorry to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the record show that again today we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis in the absence of Judge David, who is involved in another case, Lukic and Lukic. Thank you so much. I am sorry, I should have said at that at the beginning, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Certainly, not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in the context of being a diplomat, there are many considerations that you underwent in terms of forwarding the positions that you felt were important for your country; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And among other things, you had to make determinations about such things as what member states or nations you could obtain as allies for your position; true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly in part.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What member states or nations would be your opponents? And I'm speaking now in a diplomatic sense, not the sense of a Clausewitzian concern?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think as a good diplomat you try to keep that to a minimum, if at all. You try to maintain also communications -- as you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. There's a recognition that there are independent concerns and interests of the various participants in the diplomatic dialogue; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to your efforts, it would be fair to say, for example, that one of the groups within the context of a diplomatic ally that you had was the OIC, which is something that we've discussed before; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the issue of Russia, you commented on some questioning asked by Ms. Bolton the other day that often times, and if I'm going too far, please let me know, often times Russia took the position that was allied with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I prefer to use the word sometime "sympathies" which is a lot more vague in what positions may have been undertaken by any one country.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Within the context of the diplomatic jargon, does "sympathy" have any particular significance? Is it a term of art as used amongst you folks?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, actually, I would say not in this case. It's just maybe a personal observation, and one that gave, obviously, the opportunity for Russia and many other states that might not always have been sympathetic to Bosnia, that in fact they did take positions also that were, I think, helpful in trying to resolve the crisis, the anti-aggression, and the genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to statements made, and at this time I'm speaking about generally, oftentimes statements that were made with regard to the pressing issues at hand - and for example, I'm going to return to 71.3, Resolution that is - were made in private as between diplomats; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And there was an understanding that you obtained over your tenure at the United Nations that there was a body of thought that that particular resolution did not apply, as you've told us before, to Bosnia-Herzegovina because Bosnia-Herzegovina had not been in existence at the time of its passing; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, as a recognised member state.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the issue then that exists as to whether or not the resolution would have any effect upon you, and by you I mean Bosnia, there was a view that it was inappropriate for you to be held under the strictures of that particular resolution by a number of your allies; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, there was a competing view that existed during the tenure of your ambassadorship during the conflict, and that competing view was that as a, and I'm going to put it in these terms, as a geographical matter, any nation, state or entity -- and the reason I'm doing that, I think, is self-evident, because of -- there were the Republic of Srpska and the Republic of Srpska Krajina that were claimed also as nation-states during that time, whether you agree or disagree with the validity of their creation, that geographically all political entities that existed in the former Yugoslavia were under the strictures of 713; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with the statement that all of the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. And within the context of the territory of the former Yugoslavia, there were, among other areas defined within that territory, Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The Republic of Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That actually never came into discussion, again, because they did not have the status of either a recognised member state or someone who in fact was involved in defence against aggression and genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Slovakia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Slovenia, I think, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thank you so much, Slovenia. Thank you. It must be because it's Canada Day that I made a mistake. And happy Canada Day to all Canadians. Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Serbia, Montenegro, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And there was also an entity called the Republic of Srpska Krajina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, a non-recognised entity, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you use the term non-recognised entity, does that mean by virtue of the fact that they were a non-recognised entity, they were in your estimation, by your estimation, I'm referring to you as a diplomat for Bosnia-Herzegovina, not under consideration nor part of the discussion with regard to the solution of the former territory of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, actually, I would not make that broad statement. First of all, they were not recognised by any member state of the United Nations, nor were they recognised as having any sort of international status. On the other hand during numerous negotiations on behalf of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I and other, obviously, representatives of the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina did in fact engage directly sometimes, frequently indirectly with negotiations of those who represented themselves as being representatives of a certain internal, if you would, institution, internal designation, whatever in fact that may eventually evolve to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey, we would like to finish. When Mr. Guy-Smith suggested political entities within the former Yugoslavia were bound by this resolution, you said, no, you said territory. Do you accept that territory of the RSK and the territory of the RS is part of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that, therefore, Resolution 713 would apply to them equally by virtue of the fact that they are part of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would you agree with the following proposition: That an agreement between governments can be defined as an exchange of conditional promises by which each party declares that it will act in a certain way on condition that the other parties act in accordance with their promises. Sanctions supported by a higher authority cannot be invoked in case of a violation as they can for contracts under domestic law, nonetheless, these promises are significant since the parties have an interest in living up to them for other reasons.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may be obligations that have a reciprocal nature, that is, reciprocity. And if that's the way you use conditionality, I agree. Of course other agreements may have an absolute nature to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the issue of the absolute nature of them, with your contact with other member states, did you have, during your tenure as an ambassador, agreements on behalf of Bosnia-Herzegovina that had an absolute nature to them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is fair to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, areas where, from the time that you began your tenure as the ambassador until Dayton where there was not an agreement with an absolute nature, were such things as the map; correct? That was a topic of ever-changing discussion?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would disagree with that, Mr. Guy-Smith. I think once Bosnia was accepted as a member state, it was accepted within the notion of its territorial integrity and sovereignty. That was not a matter to be tested from the outside by any neighbour or other state. It could only be discussed in the context of any sort of internal territorial delineation as regions, potentially, or as we have in Canada, provinces, or in the United States, as we have states, or as we have in many other situations some form of municipal --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact, Mr. Sacirbey, that there were a number of discussions about changing the contours of the map, both under the Vance Owen plan as well as private discussions that you had with various representatives of member states; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never in the context of changing international borders, at least that I'm privy to, and to the extent that some one may have wished to initiate them, I would not engage in such. I am not privy, as a Bosnian official, to any of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Isn't it at that fact that -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey, isn't it a fact that with regard to the Vance Owen plan, there were discussions concerning the nature and the contours of the boundaries?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not international boundaries, only the internal delineation. In fact, there was a notion whether it would be either 9 cantons or 12 cantons. What the boundaries, not borders, of those cantons might be, and even what the political nature of those cantons might be, but not international borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to private conversation, which I mentioned, you had specific private conversations in which you were urged to trade, for example, the enclaves in the eastern section for Sarajevo, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but again in the context of whether it was the Federation or Republika Srpska, but both of those entities being in the context of the international borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the trade of the eastern enclaves for Sarajevo, who did you have that discussion or those discussions with?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was approached, and again, I never initiated, and I would have, and always did, reject that notion, those approaches came from Carl Bildt.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Stop for a minute, please. For purposes of the record, when you say Carl Bildt, who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Carl Bildt is the current foreign minister of Sweden. At one time he was in fact the prime minister of Sweden. During this tenure, I believe he was, most of the time, the designated moderator of the European Union. I use the word moderator or representative in the context of the talks on the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apart from Carl Bildt, who else had the discussion with you with regard to the trading of the eastern enclaves for Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Sacirbey. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just again, with respect to the rules of cross-examination, there was some discussion in examination-in-chief with the witness of a request that the enclaves be traded after the fall of Srebrenica, not specific, though, to Sarajevo, so terms of the scope of cross-examination, unless it's certainly outside the scope of direct examination, and then there's just simply the issue of relevance of this line of questioning if it is outside the scope of direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, if it was discussed, that there were that kind of discussion and the Defence has a different understanding of that discussion, surely it's up to them to put their understanding to the witness. If their understanding is that that discussion took place in the context of a trade-off of Sarajevo, and that was not the case with the Prosecution, they must put their understanding to the witness, shouldn't they? And the witness can just say, no, that was not so; or, yes, it was so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. I'm actually not feeling too well at the moment. If I could just have a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, you're not. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No, I am sorry. My stomach is acting up, and I wonder if I could just have maybe a 5-minute recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may. Do you have Mr. Harmon taking over your objections on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Well, I haven't spoken to him. I just want to go take something to settle my stomach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just go, Madam. I don't know what we are going to do. Mr. Harmon, do you want to take up that objection, or do you want to stay? Do you want us to wait for Madam Bolton?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would prefer waiting for Ms. Bolton to return. She'll be back within two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hope so. Sorry, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's perfectly all right. It seems the nature of this examination. So where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No comment. This is a very peculiar situation. I think the time is a little too long for us to be sitting here. At the same time I'm mindful of the fact that we are one-sided, the one leg is missing completely. I was going to suggest a short adjournment rather than sitting here. I'm sure people can do much more productive work talking freely, not felling like you're in court and preparing other things than just whispering around.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would appreciate that. That seems like a sensible course to me. We will be on stand-by or close about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Javier, you will be a witness to the Prosecution that we talked nothing about the case. Court adjourned. --- Break taken at 2.51 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, how is Madam Bolton? Is she improving?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, she is indisposed at the moment. If we could take our normal break at 3:30, I will be in a better position to inform the Court, but I'm prepared to proceed in her absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Story you down there. It was an emergency, and I'm not quite sure whether we made you aware that we were adjourning when we did adjourn. We are very sorry about that. Mr. Harmon, Madam Bolton was in the middle of objecting when she left. I don't know whether you want to pursue the objection or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, sir. We will withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Guy-Smith, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My last question had been ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear it too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm having some background noise. That was the reason I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is a what I'm saying. I'm hearing, too, the background -- and I think it's because of the connection to New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I'll try to proceed with it -- I'll try to proceed and see how it goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My last question had been apart from Carl Bildt, who else had the discussion with you with regard to the trading of the eastern enclaves for Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most specific that I can be is the Dutch defence minister. And it was very much in the context of the situation of the enclave themselves, and he was also very clear that in fact he was being urged by quote/unquote "his European colleagues" and US colleagues to press that matter. The issue may have been raised in some negotiating process that I'm not entirely privy to, but that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm only asking you things for the moment that you are either privy to or aware of. With regard to the Dutch defence minister, who were you referring to there? Was that Mr. Voorhof that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and, again, I want to be very specific here because there may be some confusion. I'm talking now about before the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you have discussions with Mr. Holbrooke concerning the issue of exchanging Sarajevo for the eastern enclaves?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This only occurred after the fall of Srebrenica and in the context of the Dayton Accords, which I believe I had described during direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: He, in fact, pressed us, urged us, you can use whichever term you want, that in fact Srebrenica could not be retained in the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And apart from Mr. Holbrooke, Mr. Bildt and Mr. Voorhof, are there any other individuals who you had this specific conversation with? And that, once again, is the trading of the eastern enclaves for Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again to be very precise, nothing from certainly before the fall of Srebrenica until the fall of Srebrenica when it became obviously a significant topic of the negotiating process through Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just for a moment since you mentioned here in your answer Mr. Bildt. With regard to Mr. Bildt and Srebrenica, did you have -- you had discussions with Mr. Bildt concerning Srebrenica prior to its fall, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is in fact the emphasis of what I think I had just answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, I see. And if I'm not mistaken, it's your contention that Mr. Bildt told you that he would not, and by he, I mean the United Nations, would not defend Srebrenica from attack; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That specific conversation actually occurred on the day that Srebrenica was falling, that was being overrun.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say that specific conversation, the conversation that you referring to is a conversation in which Mr. Bildt told you that the United Nations would not defend Srebrenica; correct? That's your position; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And in that --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position is that he said -- sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in that regard --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position is that Mr. Bildt said at that time that he would not depend Srebrenica, nor Zepa, no Gorazde; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to that, you were -- it's your position that you were calling for air-strikes and Mr. Bildt refused to allow for those air-strikes to occur; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's an oversimplification, but, in general, I can accept that. Yes, I can accept that characterization.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take that it would be fair to say that you are not particularly fond of Mr. Bildt's position with regard to this issue?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Because I believe it contributed to the consequences of the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to, and now I'm going to move for a moment to Mr. Holbrooke, with regard to the issue of territory - and now I'm changing the conversation slightly from that of exchange to that of obtaining territory - there came a time, and if I'm not mistaken, it was in Zagreb, although I may be, and please help me if I'm wrong, where you met with Mr. Holbrooke, and he encouraged you to take Prijedor militarily; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. It happened on more than one occasion, and in fact, once involving President Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to it happening on more than one occasion, could you please tell us the dates that this occurred where Mr. Holbrooke encouraged you to take Prijedor militarily?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the relevance of this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, the relevance of this line of questioning is that it is part of the entire picture with regard to the information that would necessarily have been, or could have necessarily been had by my client and was one of the issues that needs to be considered in the context of the entirety of the discussion over what he thought and what he did. And if I might, I believe that the discussion between Mr. Holbrooke and Mr. Sacirbey, as it relates to this particular issue and as it's going to relate to other particular issues, is part of the private diplomatic dialogue that we were discussing before. And it's our contention that the diplomatic dialogue and the resolutions that have been discussed with Mr. Sacirbey operate in what I'll call a parallel universe. They co-exist, and they sometimes converge with each other. And if there's going to be assumptions made that General Perisic knew about a certain kind of evidence or a certain kind of information, which we have thus far seen in the nature of broadcast media and united resolutions, which were distributed through the member states, then another legitimate discussion and assumption to be made is that the parties to this discussion, including the member states, the United Nations Security Council, and the countries who were affected by this debate were kept informed about it. The diplomatic debate that I'm referring to here is a diplomatic debate that would necessarily affect all of the entities or nations in the region including FRY. And the information is information that is intelligence information, cables. We've actually seen some of the cable information, Your Honour, in terms of the cables that were sent by various Russian -- not Russian, excuse me, by various attaches or diplomats concerning the events that, as they were transpiring, in which it was noted whether or not General Perisic was on or was not on the distribution list, intercepts, meetings. And I think in the context of what we are dealing with right now, it would be extremely misleading and wouldn't be the truth to suggest that the kind of evidence we've seen thus far represents the entirety of the diplomatic dialogue. The social or political and military reality at the time, all of which are issues and all of which is information that necessarily would go into the thought processes of all of the participants, and in specific, into the thought process of General Perisic to create the impression that the political military leaders make decisions solely on the kind of evidence we've been presented to -- or with by the Prosecution. And the media reports alone I think is not only incorrect, but it's unreasonable and, indeed, irrational. And this kind of information -- and by that I'm referring to the information in which I think it's recognised. And I think if this were to be developed with Mr. Sacirbey, he would agree, whether he would readily agree or not, I don't know, but he would agree that the obtaining of territory is one of the aspects that falls into the entire negotiation process. I talked to him briefly about the -- and I'm still in that conversation about the trade of Sarajevo for the enclaves, about the changing contours of the map, and, clearly, the issue of Prijedor is the one of the issues that deals with the changing contours of the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, one and a half pages of the screen in response to an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ends up not explaining your argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm trying to get the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't want you to give me another long speech. You know, Mr. Harmon said relevance, one word. And you can just say in maybe three sentences how relevant it is. The more you explain, the more you lose me. Looking at what you have just said, it seems to me that in any case in this Tribunal, it would then be relevant to talk about anything that took place from Slovenia to Montenegro in any case, and that becomes relevant because it's all in the context of this whole war within the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm not being that expansive. But I'm dealing with a discrete time-period. The discrete time-period that I'm dealing with in terms of the conflict and in terms of the period of time in which my client is charged with behaviour that is deemed criminal includes this particular time-period. It's in this particular time-period, pre-Dayton, if there are events that occurring that can affect his thinking process, and one of them would be the taking of -- the taking of territory in another area and how he may or may not respond to that, then that's relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My point precisely, that in fact, time-periods and area, territory, as I say, from Slovenia to Montenegro --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not dealing with any of that, Your Honour. What I'm talking about is -- [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I'm saying, looking at the logic of your argument here, this is what comes to mind, and I -- for purposes of this and purposes of progress, I'm going to disallow the objection. Just go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, my question was: Could you tell us the dates that your discussion occurred with Mr. Holbrooke in which he encouraged you to take Prijedor militarily?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in the early fall of 1995, after the NATO air-strikes had started and before, in fact, there was a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Apart from -- apart from those particular areas that we've discussed which is at this point the trade of Sarajevo for the enclaves and the taking of Prijedor, were you encouraged by Mr. Holbrooke in the early fall of 1995 after the NATO air-strikes to engage in other -- any other military actions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I'm going to object on the relevance of a private conversation that took place between Mr. Sacirbey and Mr. Holbrooke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where do we have it, Mr. Harmon, that it was a private conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The earlier testimony -- I'll find it in just a minute, Your Honour. I'll find it, Your Honour, in just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Rather than take up the time, why don't I ask a preparatory question. I'll honour my friend 's concern for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fine, if you honour his concern, okay, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I should say Mr. Harmon's concern, because I come from another tradition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were the conversations that -- the conversations that we were just discussing, which is, apart from the taking of Prijedor, conversations that were private as between you and Mr. Holbrooke?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: At times they may have involved other officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say at times they may have involved other officials, who would those other officials have been, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at least in one instance, I have referred to President Izetbegovic being, obviously, the primarily participant in that discussion. At other times that were other officials of what was then the US delegation to the peace process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what effect did the presence of those other officials have on the discussions with respect to whether the discussions were private or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I'm not hearing you at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Really?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you hear me? Can you hear me in New York? They don't hear me either. Are you in New York.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honour, we can't hear you at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can't hear me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it doesn't appear that the microphone -- oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We can't hear one another even here. Don't worry. Can you hear me, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] We can hear you now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, only if I take off my earphones can I hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want me to go on with your earphones off? At least you don't need any interpretation from the English to your language.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not yet. No, I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're fine. I was saying, Mr. Sacirbey, what effect does the presence of President Izetbegovic and other officials during these meetings have with respect to the status of the meeting being either private or not private?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honour, I can never be certain to what extent Mr. Holbrooke or others were speaking in the context of the States they represented or expressing potentially just personal views. That is the only reservation I have. Otherwise, the meetings were, one would say, in private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Even with the presence of other officials?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] They were not meetings that would necessarily have a minute-taker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You just indicated there was meetings that would not necessarily have a minute-taker. Are you aware of -- well with regard to your reactions, first of all, after you were involved in these private meetings, did you have discussions with others concerning the nature of those meetings? For example, with your --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: For example, your military officers in which you told them --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you told them something to the effect, did you not, that you had had a conversation with American representatives, and they indicated that they were -- they wished for you to --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, now, I cannot hear anything. You have all of a sudden gone completely off.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Could we try to reconnect or whatever we do, whatever we do here. We are close to the break, so perhaps it could be done during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, we'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned, while we reconnect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I apologise, Your Honours, before you go on, we cannot hear anything that is happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You cannot hear anything? You don't hear? You don't hear? Obviously we are disconnected. Perhaps might be cheaper for the Chamber to go to New York.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I suggest we wait so that when it comes on, we take a maximum advantage of the time it works.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We can hear you now. And can you hear us? You can't hear us? Can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, we don't hear it. Oh, yeah, now we can. Now we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We can hear you too. Thank you so much. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you told members of your military that you had had conversations with American representatives, and they had indicated that they wished for you to take certain territory; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a conversation with President Izetbegovic on this point; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apart from President Izetbegovic, did you have conversations with anyone else concerning this particular matter, that being the suggestion that you engage in military activities?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: At some point in time with General Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you had the conversation with Rasim Delic, I take you indicated to him the same thing that you told President Izetbegovic with regard to the taking of Prijedor and other areas; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I apologise, Your Honours, we are having technical difficulties again. Incoming video is frozen, and we don't hear any sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am sorry, Madam Registrar, I really don't know what to do now. Are they gone?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe that Madam Registrar is going to be calling Mr. Registrar in a moment. It looks like she's making a telephone call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You still can't hear us, Madam Registrar, out in New York? It's getting to an unacceptable stage. I'm not quite sure --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would reluctantly suggest that we take a break and that the technicians on both sides of the ocean engage in whatever technological discussions they can have or technological fix-its or repairs or Scotch tape, or whatever else works so that we can proceed in a fashion. It's been close to two hours, and I don't think I've been ability to get more than five questions out at any one given point. Although I may be exaggerating, I don't think I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you think, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I share the view of Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's take a break. Now, they've disappeared even from the screen. I just wanted to say to them we are taking a break, if they can hear me, and if they are not going to hear me, if I could see them, I would give them some sign language. Okay, we can't see them, we are going to take a break. And will be called, when we are called. --- Break taken at 4.07 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's hope technology works now. Mr. Guy-Smith. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Being an eternal optimist, I just want to make sure that I understand one thing. When are we going to take the next break assuming for purposes of discussion that we get that far?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The next break was supposed to be at quarter past 5.00. Let's carry on --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's fine. Okay. Wonderful. That's wonderful.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We were last talking about your discussion with General Delic concerning the taking of territory pursuant to the suggestion made by Mr. Holbrooke and other, as I understood it, representatives of the American government. When did you have that conversation with General Delic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably sometime subsequent to the conversations with President Izetbegovic and myself, and Holbrooke at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say sometime subsequent, obviously one of the issues was, I take it, a question of whether or not there was a perception internationally that your campaign to take these territories, and specifically Prijedor, was tied into the NATO air-strikes. And you had been informed by Mr. Holbrooke that that was something that they did not want to have occur in the international eye; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is largely correct. I wouldn't have quite characterised it that way, but that's largely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So part of the concern that Mr. Holbrooke discussed with you, which you discussed with President Izetbegovic was the importance of it seeming to the world that this was an independent action on the part of the Bosnian-Herzegovinian government; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Guy-Smith, I would character -- [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Mr. Harmon is is on his feet. Hold on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, again I have a relevance objection to this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Simply put, we are charged in an indictment in which we have repeatedly objected to its temporal scope and its geographic scope. We are, as a matter of fact, probably charged in the largest indictment that has been charged at the Tribunal. Three separate cases have been charged, three separate incidents. This particular issue is an issue which is germane to our Defence; it's germane to an examination by this Chamber of what was going on and what information was available and what potentially was the thinking process of our client. We have asked for there to be limitations, they have been denied repeatedly. We are speaking about an issue that deals with the discrete period of time that we are -- that we actually in fact have concerns about, and it is certainly relevant to our Defence and we should be entitled to develop it. We did not bring this indictment. We did not bring these charges, and we cannot be placed in the situation where we are continually foreclosed from developing evidence that would allow for you people to make a determination of what is appropriate with regard to this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, in one sentence, can you tell us how, to what point in the case is this line of questioning relevant. You know -- [overlapping speakers]... that's why I said, we might as well talk about the entire former Yugoslavia and the entire period.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, quite frankly, in a certain sense, that's what we have been charged with. Unfortunately, that's not our fault. We've asked for that not to occur. But with regard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just in one sentence, tell us what point is it relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. It's relevant to issues concerning his intent and his mens rea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any response, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, my objection stands. This is a conversation with between Mr. Holbrooke and Mr. Izetbegovic. And what the importance was to the world's perception, I don't see how that is relevant to any issue that's before this Chamber and that is in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I must rule you out of order at this point. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are the concerns that you discussed with Mr. Holbrooke concerns that you discussed with General Delic in terms of the planning of taking over these territories?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such concerns were primarily to the consequences for all the civilian population of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Frankly, I was not concerned about global perception; I was concerned about the consequences for all of the population, as well as the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So I take it you answer to my question, then, would be, no, you did not discuss the concerns that have been voiced to you by Mr. Holbrooke with your general?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not have discussed that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I would like to move now for a moment into a definition and see whether or not you agree or disagree with this definition. And that refers to the definition of a safe area. The idea of a safe area or sanctuary is an old concept in war where both sides, parties to a conflict, agree they will not fight in an area to preserve the civilian population in that area, and that would, therefore, be a safe area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are asking me do I understand that to be a definition of a UN safe area, I must say that I'm not at all certain. I'm not at all certain that there was ever an absolute consensus regarding that definition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. When you say that there was not a consensus regarding that definition, would you agree that in order for an area to be considered to be a safe area with the concomitant protections that such an area would have, that it had to be demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I believe you understand, Mr. Guy-Smith, from the direct testimony, the declaration of Srebrenica as a safe area was actually not conditional upon it being demilitarised. There was only a subsequent arrangement -- [overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Excuse me, sir, excuse me, sir. We are doing it again. You are not answering my general question. I didn't ask you anything about Srebrenica at this point. I asked you about the concept of a safe area.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the answer is I would not necessarily agree. I could, but not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right. Would it be fair to say that with regard to your definition of a safe area that your definition takes into account particular geographic territories of which you were concerned about during your tenure as ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It took into consideration geographic delineations and also what commitment was made it to actually defend those territories by those that had declared them safe areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say what commitment was made by those who had declared them safe areas, I take it that you are referring to two main Security Council resolutions; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring of course to UN as well as NATO commitments and the actual willingness or capacity to enforce those; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right. With regard to the issue of UN, I take it that in that sense you are referring to Resolutions 824 and 836; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several other resolutions, there was a series of them, but those two would be included.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And would you agree that those resolutions had the effect of defining Gorazde, Sarajevo, Tuzla, Bihac, Zepa, and I believe it was Maglaj as safe areas?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe -- I'm not sure about Maglaj that you just included, that was one of the discussions once.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Maglaj was a discussion point. That is correct. You're right. Now, with regard -- with regard to those areas that were designated as safe areas, it was understood by UNPROFOR, was it not, that those areas were to be demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe -- again I have to qualify that the word demilitarised was used, and at the same time, in fact, it was frequently taken into consideration that at least certain defence forces would in fact be in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In other words, let's say for Sarajevo, there was never a requirement that either the military forces of the Bosnian government or even their weapons would in fact be removed from the safe area. They were, as you will recall in Sarajevo, for example, there were points where heavy weapons were gathered, and they in fact, I think the same model was used in Srebrenica and the models varied a little from safe area to safe area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to Srebrenica, isn't it true that there was a demilitarisation agreement signed for that specific area?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. There was one signed. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when was that signed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was signed exactly around the same time that the resolution on Srebrenica being declared a safe area was adopted, and it was actually signed independent of that resolution, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Who were the signatories to that agreement, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recall only that of course the UN forces on the ground, along with the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Serbian forces besieging the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the Serbian forces besieging the area, as you've defined them, were at that time, if I'm not mistaken, led by Ratko Mladic; true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And do you recall that it was Ratko Mladic who in fact signed this particular agreement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly, I don't, but it could very well have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There was a point of contention after this agreement was signed by virtue of the fact that Srebrenica was not demilitarised, wasn't there? Irrespective of whether --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a point of discussion on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This was a point of contention with regard to whether or not it should be defined as a safe area because in fact there was a standing military presence in that particular enclave; true? Irrespective of --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was not an issue as to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Irrespective of its strength?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I believe your question has several assumptions made into it, that's why I'm answering it. I don't think there was a discussion as to whether or not Srebrenica should be a safe area. There was a discussion to what extent in fact it had been demilitarised to the extent that either the resolution or any other methodology required.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, with regard to the resolutions at hand, and by that I'm referring to 824 and 836, it was very clear what the limitations were of the UNPROFOR peacekeeping force in that area; true? And by that I mean --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: By that I mean the limitations were -- they could protect the area; they could not defend the area. The best that they could do was to deter attacks against by their presence, which was not a war-fighting mission, but, rather, is a peacekeeping mission; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that -- let me rephrase this. The mandate of UNPROFOR was something that was dynamic. And it's one of the issue that gave me, frankly, pause. Because at least in my role as an ambassador of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the United Nations, it was my view that the commitment given there was one to defend and protect the area and the population in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. I've understood what you've said, and I've understood you've also said that it was dynamic. And with regard to the issue of it being dynamic, the language that was utilized was "to use all means possible to deter attacks against;" correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And that is now language that has precedent, and in the past has been used in very broad terms, for example, for the liberation of Kuwait.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that. But I think if we have a discussion concerning Kuwait, both you and I would obtain considerable ire from the Chamber. So I'm not going to have a discussion with you concerning Kuwait at this time. However, with regard to the language that we just were referring to, to use all means possible to deter attacks against, that language depended on the cooperation of both parties to the conflict here, not to either attack out or attack in because United Nations --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it depends --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Because the United Nations forces, themselves, were not in a military position to defend or protect; correct? And I'm dealing with both attacking out as well as attacking in.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe first of all, Mr. Guy-Smith, they were supposed to be in a position to defend and protect. And in part, of course, this was the relationship with NATO that was in fact interwoven eventually. Now, the reason I use dynamic is because in fact there were numerous discussions that came about as to what in fact should be the nature of that demilitarised zone, and of course what are in fact the measures that might trigger response in protection of the safe area, and the what was then also defined as the NATO protected zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I want to go back here for a moment to deal with the agreement for demilitarisation of Srebrenica, and that's P2462, if we can please have that up on the screen. And I need to have page 15 which is annex two of that document. It's going to be a document that you are going to find -- we have to put it up on the screen for you, too, sir. So this will be an e-court document for you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: First of all, can you see the document? You seem to be scrunching your eyes. So do you need to have it bigger?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, we do need to bigger, but we do have it in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a touch bigger.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think you might find it at 15K of the Prosecution binder, if you have that binder available to you. Yes, here. It's your binder; we don't have a binder.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can also read it, it's fine. I can read it now off the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Can counsel please repeat the page number again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. It's page 15. And I believe that it's in the Prosecution binder. It's tab 15K for the year 1993. Madam Registrar, it might be in either 15F or 15K, but I'm happy to work off the screen, whatever makes your life easier. I'm just trying to make your life a bit easier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Mr. Guy-Smith, I can read it off the screen now, so you can proceed if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: First of all, are you familiar with the individuals who are mentioned in the very first prefatory paragraph of the agreement for demilitarisation of Srebrenica, those being General Mladic, General Halilovic, and Lieutenant General Wahlgren representing UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Guy-Smith. Our screen doesn't show those names. Can we please be shown that page with Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, it's -- sure. I'm sorry, Your Honour. I thought everybody was on the same page. Apparently not. That's 15 of 19, page 15 of 19. Is that of assistance, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I have the -- in front of me, Mr. Guy-Smith. What I thought was on the screen, but I'm not sure I know which section you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you see where it says Annex 2 at the very top of the page? Agreement for demilitarisation of --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. No, I do not. No, I do not. I don't have that page in front of me that's on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. If we could have Mr. Registrar transmit that page electronically across the ocean so that Mr. Sacirbey is looking at the same document that we are looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's the date of the -- the date of the document is 30 April 1993. It's the report of the Security Council mission established pursuant to Resolution 819 (1993). And we are referring to 15 of 19 pages.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see Annex 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I can, with some difficulty, read the language of that. If that could be magnified just a little bit, I think I'll have an easier time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Now it just needs to be clarified. I just need to have it focused. Yes, I can read it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And my question to you, sir, is do you recognise the individuals who are mentioned as being present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And could you tell us who Lieutenant Wahlgren was, in your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him as one of the UN commanders. I don't remember his exact position, the hierarchy. He was not the commander, but he was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to this particular agreement, as I understand it, I'm now looking at the first numbered paragraph. Indicates that: "A total cease-fire in the Srebrenica area effective from 0159 on 18 April 1993, freezing all combat actions on the achieved lines of confrontation including supporting artillery and rocket fire." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And then I'm going to move to paragraph 4 in which it indicates that: "The demilitarisation of Srebrenica will be complete within 72 hours of the arrival of the UNPROFOR company in Srebrenica with a designated time of 1100 hours, 18 April 1993." With a caveat of course that if UNPROFOR arrives at a later time, this will be changed. And I think it would be fair to interpret that meaning the 72-hour period would be changed. It would be conditioned upon the arrival of UNPROFOR to the area.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see your reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the language that's contained herein, that being the demilitarisation, do you interpret that to mean something other than getting rid of the weapons of war in that area?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I think you will recall, this is not an agreement with which I worked with, nor any other representative in the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not my question, sir. Not -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Second of all -- [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey, you are doing it again. And it really does not behoove you to do this. With regard to the language that is contained herein, that being demilitarisation, do you interpret that to mean something other than getting rid of the weapons of war in that area, yes or no? And thereafter you can explain.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time there was never enforcement, as I understand it, even of light weapons, that is, weapons that were carried on the side by the defenders or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you agree that there were Bosnian forces in Srebrenica who went out of Srebrenica on missions, and by missions I mean military missions?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly if that was the case, I was not aware of it at the time. Now, clearly that's been a discussion point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say clearly that's been a discussion point, you mean clearly that's been a discussion point in the conversation that you and I are having right now today, or clearly that was a discussion point sometime in your history as an ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, there have been other events proceedings before the Tribunals that have discussed that point. And second of all, yes, it has been also a point of discussion during my tenure as ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to this issue, the issue of demilitarisation of Srebrenica is one of the -- is one of the areas where you had points of contention with none other than, I believe it was General Rose; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to recall the specific point that you are addressing. Would you care to be more specific on that, or are you expecting a broad answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, at the moment I'm asking for a broad answer, if you are able to give us one.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the point of issue always was that safe area included not only the defence of protection but also enabling humanitarian supplies to reach it, And in fact this safe area would not be strangled. The definition of what weapons would be allowed, I believe over time, over time became rather standard, which was heavy weapons. And as I understand it in Srebrenica all the heavy weapons in fact were taken into holding areas by the United Nations forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: One of the things that you seem to mention throughout your testimony, which actually makes, I think, a great deal of sense, is you talk about situations being dynamic and things changing over time; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, that is a natural consequence of conflict; true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would prefer not to say natural, but unfortunately I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would prefer not to say it either, but since we still have failed to outlaw war, I think it's something we that need to recognise. With regard to the issue of the dynamic aspect of the conflict, would you agree that in your diplomatic capacity, you were constantly confronted with in having to deal with an ever-changing situation on the ground militarily?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There's nothing particularly --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can add that sometimes I thought beside what was happening on the ground, there was a cynicism that allowed facts to be created on the grounds in order to somehow facilitate some of the solutions offered by the mediators. I think there was a lot of cynicism -- all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say there was a lot of cyncism, the cyncism that you are referring to, as I understand your answer, encompassed the mediators. And who would those be?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would certainly not leave Belgrade out of this -- but you are right. I include here also some of the mediators that were are involved. And, unfortunately, I believe it did not help eventually bring about a solution that was consistent with international legality and erasing the consequences of aggression and genocide. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you refer to the mediators, you are discussing such people as we mentioned here before as Mr. Bildt and Mr. Holbrooke; correct? Those are the individuals that you are discussing with with regard to the cynicism?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, I've never hidden that term. That is correct, I've never hidden that term. I'm on the record on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would you -- let me ask you this: Are you familiar with the term as it exists for negotiations between nations of what is called a normalization agreement or normalisation process?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to say something to you and see whether you agree or disagree with the following: In situations where fighting will continue or threatens to resume unless agreement is reached, public opinion and other domestic forces may exert considerable pressures on the negotiators to agree. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the point. I'm not sure why I would agree or disagree with it now, though. But I understand the point. It's a relevant point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in terms of it being a relevant point, it's clearly one of the things that you take into account -- oh, I'm sorry, that you took into account during the time that you were a diplomat and your tenure at the United Nations; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I think we -- besides reacting, we also have the obligation to initiate, obviously, positive dynamics in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to what you've just said, I think it would be fair to say, would it not, that there are often important asymmetries in the susceptibility of the various negotiators to such pressures; true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And as a matter of fact, one of the things that you did, and I think quite effectively, was that you created a plan that allowed for pressures to exist to influence public opinion. And I'm not saying this in a critical way whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's a compliment, I'll taking it. But I think you can best make the assessment yourself and so can the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, apart from the issue of the pressures for agreement, would you agree that negotiations for the purpose of a normalisation are strongly influenced by what I would call the instability of the, and I put this in quotes, abnormal situation they are supposed to settle, for example, a war?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the problems that I had with your line of reasoning here is that Belgrade is not just reacting. In fact, it is very much an actor in this plight.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Once again, once again, Mr. Sacirbey -- once again, Mr. Sacirbey, I didn't mention Belgrade. And I know you have a tendency to go there. And I know you've lived your life going there, but that's not the question I'm asking you. I'm asking you a different question at this time.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead, I maybe misunderstood it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The negotiations for the purpose of normalisation are strongly influenced by the instability of the abnormal situation they are supposed to settle; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Would you agree that if fighting continues while negotiations are prolonged, one side may gain, through force, what it failed to gain through bargaining?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may in fact be the case, and that's where I think the cynicism can come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right. And with regard to the cynicism, that, for example, would be part and parcel the discussion that we were having as it related to Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If in fact the idea of fighting was to create facts on the ground that would be forced upon the parties in negotiations, then I'm not sure he see the purpose of the death of the civilians and soldiers and the suffering that might be inflicted there --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand -- Mr. Sacirbey, Mr. Sacirbey, Mr. Sacirbey, please, try to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that the answer that was given by Mr. Sacirbey was cut off. He did give a complete answer, and it was -- you can see at line 11 page 42, it is incomplete. I think for the purposes of the record, I think it should be complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think that this is the continued problem with Mr. Sacirbey, is that he does not like to answer the question posed, but, rather, wishes to answer the question as most politicians and diplomats do, that they believe they feel like answering. And we are not having a diplomatic debate here. We are in a court of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, putting aside that observation, my observation is much more limited. There was a complete answer given; the record is now incomplete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just see. Are you saying, Mr. Harmon, that you just want that sentence complete?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Guy-Smith, obviously, Mr. Harmon just wants that sentence complete to get a complete answer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I don't believe that the answer given is - and now we are in that world that we've been in before - is relevant to the question asked. And if he is not going to answer the questions that are propounded to him, then he should be foreclosed from putting things on the record that are inappropriate. And since I'm in a different position than I was before, I will not allow for the witness to go off on a lark of his own. So from that standpoint, I believe the answer as it stands is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, Mr. Harmon, to understand how that answer answers the question immediately above it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I heard a complete answer. What is missing from the record is the complete answer. Whether it's relevant and responsive to the question that Mr. Guy-Smith asked, I don't know. All I'm asking for is that the complete answer be incorporated into the record. Obviously if it's not responsive or irrelevant, the Court can take that into consideration. Nothing more than that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think Mr. Harmon knows better, and he is playing games with the record. Mr. Harmon knows that when a witness doesn't answer a question, that's something that does not appropriately belong on the record. Now, he may well wish to have it in the record because of its emotional contents, but its emotional content is not an appropriate purpose. And to claim, as he does right now, the innocence of desiring a complete answer, I believe is somewhat disingenuous, considering that it does not answer the question propounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But I thought I heard something which -- because you both spoke at the same time, it just got drowned.
