I don't know what he said, and I'm sure that's why the stenographer also could not get it. But I see Mr. Harmon, also that the reason that answer is incomplete is because Mr. Guy-Smith was stopping him from completing it. It's not as if he was being -- he was mistakenly cut off. It's just that Mr. Guy-Smith didn't want to hear that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Guy-Smith didn't want to hear the answer, but there was an answer that has been given. Mr. Guy-Smith may not like the answer, Your Honours may not like the answer, I may not like the answer, but the record, there was an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: After the word suffering what was the rest of your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honour, I believe you are speaking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, I am speaking to you, and I don't hear you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Okay. Do you hear me now, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, now I hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Okay, Your Honour. I must admit that was not a practiced comment or speech I made, so I will try to replicate it the best that I can. And my comment was I believe that was one of the problems that I had with cynicism in this context because innocent lives of civilian soldiers and suffering were inflicted through military means that otherwise then should have been achieved through diplomatic means directly without all that unnecessary loss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That answer goes far beyond what we had heard anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And it doesn't deal with the issue that had been raised which was the issue of Prijedor, which was specifically what the question was about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I see "motor accidents" in that answer. I'm not quite sure we are talking about "motor accidents."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, at times I'm wondering whether or not it's an attempt to simplify the case to the lowest common denominator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, that's fine. Proceed Mr. Guy-Smith, before we lose contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Another aspect once again with regard to the issue of the instability of the abnormal situation is that it could well shake one's opponent's confidence in his ability to defend his military position and make him anxious to reach an agreement; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which context are we speaking now, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We are speaking in the context of diplomacy and war.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would prefer to think I engaged with diplomacy, and I think you are now going into areas that I certainly would not want to always associate myself with, which is somehow --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm saying I believe you are suggesting that as part of a diplomatic effort, there is an ongoing military effort that needs to be inflicted or carried out. And I'm not sure I would agree with that as being necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, I understand that, and I would agree with you that it's not necessarily necessary. But when dealing with an unstable situation such as a conflict, issues concerning diplomacy and war come to the front. And I believe this would be an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I had suggested we try to take advantage -- we really reconvened at half past 4.00, so we could quite easily go to quarter to 6.00 and take another break. Because, otherwise, we are going to lose connection, unless you really insist on a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I don't really insist on a break. If I have an opportunity to ask some questions and further the examination, I'm somewhat of a content human being.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to your diplomatic understandings, I'm going to ask you another general question, as to see whether you agree or disagree with this issue, which is, where there have been temporary suspension of fighting, the threat of resumption of hostilities becomes less effective for bargaining purposes, unless they are supported by existing military capabilities or preparations that make a new offensive both likely and dangerous to the opponent.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, excluding my own personal thinking, that may very well be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. When you say excluding your own personal thinking, if I'm understanding your testimony, you are desirous to divorce yourself from the inclusion of considerations about waging war in your diplomatic efforts; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not actually correct. I think that there is a different line which I'm drawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. In your capacity as an ambassador, you took into account the situation on the ground, you've told us; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You had available to you a number of differing military options that would be discussed --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- through your diplomatic efforts; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That probably is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say it's probably correct, it is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again you are saying discussed in my diplomatic capacity. I'm not sure exactly who I'm discussing it with. If you are suggesting the discussion that was had, for example, with Ambassador Holbrooke, that may be an example of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, we need to be careful with your language, because when you say "may," it becomes qualified, and we are not sure what you are saying is that that is a possibility, or what you are saying is that is something that occurred during your discussions with, for example, Ambassador Holbrooke. So when you use the word --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not -- I do not mean to use it as a qualified. When I have used it in the past, I believe during my testimony, I have frequently referred to as to what issues could have been considered as part of any situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: So in other words, at any point in time there may have been multiple considerations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And to put it in the specific terms that we are dealing with right now, the topic of varying and differing military options including, for example, NATO air-strikes, is one of the topics that you discussed with Holbrooke; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Bildt; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least to some extent, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You discussed this matter with the defence minister for the Netherlands, Mr. Voorhof, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To some extent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You discussed this matter with Madeleine Albright; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: General Rose; true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be a different, probably, context, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you that would probably be a different context, we are talking about a different point in time; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Particularly a different point in time and in the scope of General Rose's responsibility to protect and defend the civilian population, including the safe areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you took, as a matter of fact, took issue with General Rose's behaviour and decisions in that regard, did you not? And we'll be talking about a later, but just for the moment just to --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I missed that.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, in some instances I did, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it that you also discussed the matter of military options with Mr. Akashi, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at least on a couple of occasions; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And for purposes of the record, could you please identify for the Chamber who Mr. Akashi is?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi was, I cannot remember his exact starting point, but he was the civilian head of UNPROFOR, that is, the United Nations forces in the region, that is, as they were defined by the UN mandate in the region, not just for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to go back to the issue of the safe areas for a moment, if I could, and I'm going to ask you since you mentioned that you had had -- that you knew who Mr. Wahlgren was, would you agree with a statement that he made concerning the safe areas? And I'm referring now to 1D00-2536, page 2557. And for purposes of everybody's -- it's tab 55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... 1D ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: 00 -- I'm referring to page 2557. The document starts at 2536. It's a document entitled "Responsibility of command: How UN and NATO commanders influenced air power over Bosnia," by Mark A. Bucknam, colonel of the United States Air Force.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I am not sure I'm looking at the right document, but I have something in front of me. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You better make sure you have got the right document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I have page 78. And if you read a few passages, I'll be able to confirm that, Mr. Guy-Smith. I think that's what I'm suggesting. If you read a few passages, I can confirm that I have the right document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure, if you could take a look at the last paragraph: According to Michael Williams, a former director of information and senior UNPROFOR spokesman who has written about the UN's troubled political military relations; Generals Wahlgren, who I think is the gentleman that who you were referring to was present during the demilitarisation agreement of Srebrenica, and Morillon. Do you know who Morillon is?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Who is he?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is a French nationality. And the UN commander on the ground during the critical point when Srebrenica was declared a safe area. He actually, himself, travelled at that time into Srebrenica when it was under its most severe attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Guy-Smith. You have left us behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I certainly didn't mean to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We've got to paragraphs 1 to 5 of this document. That's all we see. I don't know what the heading is. It's Annex 2 agreement for the demilitarisation of Srebrenica. I thought this was a previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, no. We are in a different document. 1D00-2536 is where the document begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you are at page 2557.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm at page 2557, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, if you can go to page 2557.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could scroll down, and I believe that we will all be together now. I just asked you who Morillon was. "Had little idea how to proceed" with the implementation of the safe areas resolutions. That's something that we were discussing, I think, in slight slightly a different context when we were talking about the differences of opinion with regard to the definition of safe area.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "Honig and Both have shown that on 5 June, the day before the Security Council authorised enforcement of the safe areas, General Wahlgren prophetically warned UN political authorities in New York: "If one allowed no controls of the military or paramilitary units of the Bosnian government, one would create a scenario which would encourage the use of the safe areas as havens where forces could refit, rearm, train, and prepare for further military operations ." With regard to this particular warning, as it relates to having been made to UN political authorities in New York, was General Wahlgren's warning, indeed prophetic, a topic of discussion that you were party to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was one of the issues that gave rise to concerns about safe areas. Most importantly, obviously was the issue that I raised before, of enforcement and what in fact was being defended.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to General Wahlgren's concern about military or paramilitary units of the Bosnian government being involved and present in a safe area, were you party to those conversations? And by party to those conversations, I'm referring to those conversations of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you at that time take the position that the safe areas should not be demilitarised, because in your opinion --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- you were entitled to defend them under your analysis of, I believe it is, Chapter 51?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I continue: "Moreover, after 836 was issued, General Wahlgren worried that the safe area's concept jeopardized the impartiality of his forces in Bosnia, who were supposed to," if we could turn the page, thank you," enforce its one-sided restrictions." Was that part of the conversation that you had, the concern of General Wahlgren in this regard?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the position that you took?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our position was that, number one, the whole notion of safe areas obviously left a very big hole in the rest of the country of whether the rest of the country was a non-safe area, and in effect allowed for civilians to be actively exposed, not only to military action, but to deprivation of the necessities of life including food, water, and medicine. Number two, we were never, at that time when this was written, given obviously the necessary assurances of what measures would be used to protect that civil population, that territory. So of course, we were always trying to get clarification and in fact later commitment regarding the defence of those safe areas. And, again, to use your word, it was prophetic because in the end, Srebrenica in fact was not defended, even though the commitment was made that it would be defended.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say it was not defended, it was not defended, as far as you are concerned, by United Nations forces who had a mandate to defend it; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not by the UN forces and not by the NATO forces, which in fact were to be called upon if the area was under attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I could have Defendant's -- these particular pages admitted as defendant's next in order, I'd appreciate it, starting with 1D00-2536, which is a face-page, so there's reference. And then subsequent pages, those being 2557, and 2558.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. As separate exhibits, or just one exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: One exhibit, I think would be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Registrar, if you can give ID00-2536 an exhibit number, please, and admit it into evidence, together with other two pages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, this document shall be given Exhibit D133. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina used safe areas as locations in which BiH troops could rest, train, equip themselves, as well as fire on Serb positions which thereby provoked Serb - and by this I'm referring to Bosnian Serb - retaliation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the notion of rest, most of the soldiers were civilian soldiers, and most of them lived in that safe area. So by definition they were there. Otherwise, I'm not sure I would agree with your -- in fact I certainly not agree with elements of your broad proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say you would not agree with elements of my broad proposal, let me be clear about your disagreement with me, sir, which is that you would not agree with me that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina could train in the safe area; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that point, I am not sure what you mean by train, but I was never aware of any training being undertaken, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In a safe area?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Equip themselves --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please recall -- please recall that, for example, the safe area of Sarajevo was also in fact the headquarters of both the civilian and military forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. Equip themselves with further weaponry, do you disagree with that broad proposition as I put it to you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say not necessarily, what is your qualification, Mr. Sacirbey?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, with the one situation, at least that I'm familiar with, is Sarajevo in fact was never, the way you have defined the word, demilitarised. In fact heavy weapons were put away in UN, that is UNPROFOR holding areas, but I do not believe there was an absolute removal of all weapons from Sarajevo or any other safe area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. When I'm referring to safe areas, I'm not limiting this discussion to that of Sarajevo, sir, I'm discussing with you all safe areas. And I want the record to be clear in your understanding of my question and the intent of my question to be clear, that I'm referring to all of the safe areas that were recognised under the Resolution 824 and 836, and not just Sarajevo. Are we clear about that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do understand. I think the reason I qualified my answer to the extent that I had personal knowledge or observations of what may have been happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. From these safe areas, do you disagree with the proposition that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina fired at Bosnian Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the time-frame, that may have occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say that may have occurred, is that the qualification of the way that you generally use the word "may," or are you talking about something else?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could or could not have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, you know it did happen, don't you, Mr. Sacirbey? You know that the army of the BiH, as a matter of fact, fired from safe areas on numerous occasions throughout the conflict period?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry, is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, let me wrap it up for you. Don't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I would be happy to say, to the extent that I am aware of, in fact the -- at least some of the safe areas including Sarajevo continued to be defended by the forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina fired from those areas as in any war, such firing provoked retaliation on the part of the Bosnian Serb forces, did it not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understood your question originally was, you indicated that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had fired in order to provoke a response. I do disagree with that statement, if that is in fact the original that you made.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is the original that I did make, yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with the proposition that most of the soldiers in the Bosnian army lived inside of safe areas?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I referred -- well, that's -- let's put it this way, certainly a very large number of them did, because they were mostly civilian soldiers, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And when you use the term civilian soldiers, I find this an interesting term. Are you using the term civilian soldiers in the same way that we have discussed - and now I am going to move away from this time - non-combatants?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, actually, in here, I'm referring to the fact that most of these individuals had been recently drafted into the army, and in fact many of them -- the general situation in Bosnia was that the soldiers served for a week on the frontlines, and then had several days off with their families. They had generally limited military resources to either house them or otherwise sustain them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, if you could help us here, the leadership corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina sprang from the former JNA, did it not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Significant portion of it did, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say a significant portion of it did, can you identify for us those members of the leadership corps that sprang from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for example, General Rasim Delic, who I mentioned, General Jovan Divjak, or Colonel Siber are all of three different ethnic groups, who all had some background in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say within your knowledge that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina created a well-planned and structured organisation as any military organisation would?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the conditions, and I emphasise that conditional, given the conditions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the commander of the army, I take it, was President Izetbegovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina of which Mr. Izetbegovic was the chair.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. This would be an appropriate time because I would be moving to another subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I certainly would be. And in fact I think our tape can take us no further. We'll take a break and come back at quarter past 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to discuss with you now and turn to the issue of helicopters. First of all, it's true, is it not, that you met with a group of individuals from the Srebrenica area, I believe, in Sarajevo sometime in, I would say, early July before the fall of Srebrenica concerning their generalised worries and concern. My question to you is that they came to you from Srebrenica by which of helicopter; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who are these?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: A group of concerned citizens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] They did come to Sarajevo. I don't know how they arrived, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall discussing this matter with Mr. Nice at one point during your interview?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue of helicopters or the issue of the individuals from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I certainly -- [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am sorry, Your Honour, I was not getting sound. As I stood, I got sound. So I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, Mr. Sacirbey, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Where we left was --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was trying to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I said both. In response to your answer, the issue of helicopters or the issue of the individuals from Srebrenica, said to you both, that you discussed both of those with Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly I'm quite certain we discussed the last point, that is the delegation from Srebrenica. As to helicopters, quite possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say quite possibly, are you being speculative here, or was it within your knowledge the way that they got to you from Srebrenica was through a helicopter flight?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be clear, when I speak of helicopters, I'm aware of certainly one situation that you may be alluding to, which is, when I became foreign minister, my predecessor was shot down and killed in a helicopter being shot down. That's really what I'm referring to when we speak of helicopters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I'm referring to a different situation. I'm referring to the delegation that came to discuss matters about Srebrenica. They came to your office, I believe it was the conversation -- if this helps refresh your recollection. It was a conversation toward the end of June with President Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I very well recall that conversation and meeting with that delegation. That was in President Izetbegovic's office. But for whatever reason, I do not recall how they arrived to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to suggest something to you and see whether that refreshes your recollection in that regard, which is that you were asked by Mr. Nice, who was the delegation? How did the people get out? And you replied: "There were eight to ten people at most. We used to have helicopters that the mercenaries -- the helicopters and everything else were from the Ukraine, sometimes Russia, sometimes our own, but we really didn't have helicopters here." And then you -- do you remember that discussion with Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly remember those facts. I don't remember that discussion, but I think the way you just read that seems to imply that it was my opinion that that delegation did not come by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me ask you this, because I don't want to -- I certainly don't want to, in any sense whatsoever, mislead you here. You agree that you used to have helicopters that were from the Ukraine and sometimes from Russia, and by you I mean the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, and specifically the Bosnia-Herzegovina army in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And those helicopters were helicopters that were used by the Bosnia and Herzegovina military for purposes military and otherwise, I take it. If you know.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- that I cannot absolutely confirm for you. The one situation, as I've said, I'm very familiar with, is the shooting down of the helicopter of Dr. Irfan Ljubijankic who was flying as a Bosnian official.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware of Oric flying out of Srebrenica on a helicopter, I believe, in May of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly it is something that I was totally unaware of at the time, if that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you became aware of the fact that Oric had left -- by Oric I'm referring to Naser Oric, so the record is clear. That Naser Oric had left the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the only time I became aware of it is actually the meeting with the delegation, because he was not even present, if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, let's follow up on that just for a brief moment. Since he wasn't present with the delegation, do you know where Naser Oric was stationed after he left Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And Naser Oric, could you, for purposes of the record, please be of some assistance to us, what was his position in the army of the BiH?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly, on that point it's very difficult because, as you do know, he was not someone that either came from a JNA background or a regular backgrounds of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So, honestly, to that statement, I am not in a position to give you a better answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Were you made privy to the military reports of the army of the BiH with regard to helicopter flights in and out of various areas? And by that I mean areas where the army of the BiH was located.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think the only time I might have had some more knowledge of it would have been at the very end of the war, as is the record I flew on a helicopter into the Bihac zone after it was liberated. But, no, I was not aware of any schedule or any record-keeping regarding that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All right. After the Bihac zone was liberated, did you have occasion to see any documents concerning what I will term the air bridge of Srebrenica and Zepa that was produced by Colonel Erdin Hrustic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have a chance to see any such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The screen is locked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, we can see you and hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are told that your screen is frozen, so we don't see any movement on you. And I don't see you at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Shall we try to reconnect, maybe?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please, if you could, please. While we are waiting, how are you feeling, Madam Bolton?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We will enough to sit in the second chair, Your Honour, but thank you for your inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, I hope you get better.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, can you hear and see us now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very clearly. And can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honours, we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can. Thank you so much. Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During your tenure as ambassador, did you have contact with a gentleman by the name of Robert Fraser?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you are speaking of a US official?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to discuss with Robert Fraser any air flights for the benefit of the Bosnian army in Tuzla in early September of 1994?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I just don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall a mission that occurred, a familiarising mission, that included Ambassador Charles Thomas, Richard Holbrooke; Robert Fraser, commander brigadier General Michael Hayden [phoen] of the US Air Force, General Charles Boyd, UN Marine Corps General David Mees [phoen], US Marine Corps Lieutenant General Edward Hanlin [phoen] meeting with an army commander for the Muslim Bosnian army, Mehmet Alugic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking if I was at that meeting or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: First of all, I'm asking you if you were at that meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not at any such meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you aware of that meeting and aware that that meeting concerned the building of a secret air strip in Visoko to land heavy transport aircraft?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: At some point in time I became aware of that meeting, but certainly not, I think, any sort of current knowledge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say current knowledge, you are referring to --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The possibility of that meeting because, frankly, Mr. Guy-Smith, I must admit I've never had any sort of direct information that says who was at the meeting. I've only heard bits and pieces and much of it is speculative.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to the matter of you hearing bits and pieces, one of the individuals who I believe you would be fair to say you spent a fair amount of time with during your tenure, I believe as ambassador was Mr. Fraser; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We certainly knew each other. I wouldn't say we spent a lot of time together, no. Unfortunately, as you also know, he died on Mount Igman in August of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I know that, yes. Prior to his death is obviously the time that I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, no, I understand. And I think I'm trying to suggest to you Mr. Fraser was not someone that I dealt with extensively. Certainly I've dealt with many other US officials much more extensively.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to -- since you have raised the issue, with regard to Mr. Fraser's death, that -- as a matter of fact, the death itself, was something that Mr. Holbrooke discussed with you as being an incident that he could use for further US involvement in assisting the Bosnian Herzegovina army correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that would be correct. I think he certainly saw it as something that he could use in the context of his own efforts, but I think the last part of that conclusion is not accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The last part of the conclusion meaning in assisting the Bosnian Herzegovina army, is that what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I don't think Ambassador Holbrooke had any interest in assisting the Bosnian Herzegovinians; I think he had an interest in assisting his own mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So with regard to the unfortunate death of Mr. Fraser, you had a conversation with him, that's what I'm asking, you had a conversation with him in which he made it clear to you that he was going to be using the death of this American for purposes of furthering his particular agenda, as it related to Bosnia and Herzegovina conflict; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: He actually used that notion in the context of the death of Joe Kruzel [phoen], who is a relative of mine, a cousin of mine by marriage. So he came to me and said, Mo, your cousin is dead, somewhat excitedly, almost euphorically, and made the point that now, you know, we really had to make his mission work, because that was when the so-called US initiative for the Balkans was gaining some steam.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you are referring to --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Go ahead. I'm sorry, I didn't mean to cut you off.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit, I found it a little bit distasteful, because three very good men had just died, and including a French soldier, who I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to this particular incident, you mentioned that the so-called US initiative for the Balkans was gaining some steam. Are you referring to the attempts in the United States congress by Senator Dole to lift the embargo, or are you referring to something else?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about the process that started probably sometime that summer, not necessarily fully clear to me, which ended up in the Dayton Accord.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I understand your answer in that regard. Since we are, I believe -- could you help me here. When did that occur? When was the date of that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- I'll give you a little more. In very early August I had met with Ambassador Holbrooke and his entire team, including Bob Fraser, in Split airport because they couldn't, and they were not allowed, to land in Sarajevo, according to them, because the Serbian forces besieging the city. And we met in Split. And then they came back a week later which would have been, I believe, right around the 10th of August, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would have been which year, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I am sorry, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I want to take you back now for a moment to 1994. In 1994, if I'm not mistaken, you at some point met with a gentleman by the name of Mr. Mitterrand with Ambassador Kovac, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ambassador Kovac, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you met with Mr. Mitterrand, could you, for the purposes of the record, kindly tell us who that gentleman is.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was President Francois Mitterrand, who was the president of the French republic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And your purpose of meeting with him was to obtain his support, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, actually at that time it was to address a very dire situation that was evolving around and developing around the safe area of Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the meeting with Mitterrand, you had some concerns, and by that I mean you personally had some concerns because in your estimation, Mitterrand was a pro-Serbian and a supporter of, as you believed to be, the Serbian inclinations; correct? And I'm including all Serbs for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I found him to be more of anti-Muslim and, frankly, bigoted. That's what turned me off to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say that he was bigoted, he had a conversation with you in which he -- I'm sorry. He had a conversation with, I believe, it was the ambassador Dr. Kovac, in which --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Nikola Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Correct. And in that conversation, where you were present, you claimed that Mr. Mitterrand said it was the Muslims who were provoking the difficulties; it was the Muslims who are responsible for the difficulties; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something to that effect, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he did use -- the Muslims, as you have pointed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And it was his view -- I am sorry. I'm not asking what his view was at all because that would ask you to speculate as to what was going on in his mind. But he declared in your presence at that time in the summer of of 1994 that he was not interested in being of any assistance by virtue of the fact that it was the Muslims who were creating the problem; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure we ever reached to that concluding point. I think if you are relating the story in which I have written down on several occasions, the conclusion of that meeting was his grave rebuke to Dr. Nikola Kovac who was a Serb. And why was he in fact not with the other Serbs, and why was he a traitor to Serbs as a whole by being with the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Mr. President Mitterrand seemed to understand this conflict in ethnic terms. And I think Dr. Nikola Kovac did not. As Nikola Kovac, again, as I emphasise is a Serb himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: President Mitterrand, if I'm not mistaken, if I could be so bold, then joins that group of individuals who you are critical of in the international community, Mr. Bildt, General Rose, and Mr. Holbrooke; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the relevance of this question and this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to your encounter with Mr. Mitterrand, do you know whether or not the sentiments that you have attributed to him were voiced to others in the international community and became part of a discussion in your capacity as the ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Voiced by who?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Mitterrand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honour, I am unclear on the question as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Look at the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The issue that you attribute to Mr. Mitterrand, that Kovac was a traitor to the Serbs and that the problem that existed was a problem that existed because of the Muslims, is that something, to your knowledge, that was part of the conversations that you had in your capacity as a diplomat?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say I did not have this conversation repeated on other occasions. It was a rather unique moment especially with the head of state of, what I consider, a very progressive country, France, a multiethnic country.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you learned that the position that had been voiced in your presence by Mitterrand, was something that was part of the discussion and part of the view that was held by either the French specifically in their international capacity concerning the negotiations that were occurring at the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I'm not quite clear. Are we talking about the bigotry, the prejudice, or are we talking about some political position taken there?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, let's start with the bigotry and the prejudice, as you've defined it.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours. I object to the relevancy of that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, this actually is, certainly in our estimation, relevant because if, in fact, this, what Mr. Sacirbey claims, occurred, and that's an entirely different question, but whether or not it occurred, there's a predicate that I'm trying to figure out about which is whether or not the bigotry and prejudice that was felt by the leader of France according to Mr. Sacirbey is something that was then communicated to other members of the French delegation or any other delegation, which then would directly affect international negotiations or certainly would have that possibility. And such information, if such information existed, would be information that then would flow throughout the marketplace of ideas throughout the diplomatic community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My concern is that I was under the impression that the point under discussion at this point was neither bigotry or political position, but whether -- but the point under discussion, I thought, was Mr. Mitterrand 's alleged position that Kovac was a traitor to the Serbs, which is what was what you were discussing. And I thought when Mr. Sacirbey then says, Are you referring to bigotry or political position, he was obviously off beam and should have been brought back to the topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I believe he said bigotry or prejudice, and that's why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, I'm reading what I see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that's why I was spending a moment there because, clearly, if someone is a bigot and they have a view of others which stems from such a prejudice, then to the extent that bigotry could influence their thinking patterns and affect obviously the directions that they would give to their delegation, it would then take us to the next part which is whether or not the ambassador Kovac was, in fact, a traitor to the Serbs or not. That's what my thinking was at that point. But if that is too much, I'm happy to move on, because it's no a critical issue. I find it to be somewhat -- I'm actually somewhat taken aback by the notion that Mr. Sacirbey has indicated with regard to Mitterrand, but that's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Quite apart from, actually, the objection. For me, this whole line of -- it's just not knowing where we are going with it. Thank you so much. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After the meeting that you had with Mitterrand, in your estimation did the French position change, in any respect, in terms of support or lack of support for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly was a dynamic situation, and I'm of the view that under President Jacques Chirac, France was more constructive. At least over the long term.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, so if I understand your testimony correctly, there was a shift after Chirac came into power, which would have been when, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been in the spring of 1995. There was an inertia involved obviously in politics from past leaders to new leaders, and I think that shift did take place. We had an opportunity to meet with President Chirac in late August of 1995. And I found him to be both engaging in terms of the discussions and looking for solutions that would in fact, I think, be constructive in the context of ending the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, regard to the issue -- and we did go away from the issue unfortunately. But with regard to the issue of helicopters, I'd like to get back to that, to the whole matter of helicopters, because I believe that it was your testimony on direct that there were a number of occasions when you believed, in your capacity as the ambassador, that the air-space had been violated, and you wrote some letters in that regard; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And could you tell us as you sit here right now, where you obtained the information that you obtained with regard to your belief that the air-space that was being violated was being violated over Serbian territory or from Serbian territory.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information, as the best as I can recollect, came not only from Bosnian sources, that is, government sources, but also from the media and particularly the international forces on the ground, that is the UN forces on ground that were either responsible for monitoring, or they are in the context of peacekeepers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the information that you received, did you have occasion before testifying in court here, the opportunity to review the final report of the inquiry into unexplained radar traces between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question, I'm not sure I got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Before you came to court -- before you came to court -- obviously, they are not here. But before you came to court, did you have an opportunity to review the final report that was done with regard to this issue concerning helicopter flights? Let me make it easier for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have P2485 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yeah, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not a problem, not a problem. P2485, I believe, is a document which consists of a total of 78 pages of which you were shown the first seven, although I may have my pagination after --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] [Previous translation continues] ... identify this tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I could get some assistance from the other side of the room, I'd appreciate it. I don't have a binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you remind me of the -- oh, it's May. That would be the 1995 binder, tab 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you get that, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, we got it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I believe this document is the one where you've seen the first seven pages. We have attempted to get the balance of the document to New York in hard copy, and apparently we were not successful in that regard, so we are going to have to do this --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I have seen this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, so my first question to you is as follows, which is: Is this document a document that you saw before you testified in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to the document, when you reviewed the document, which is the inquiry into unexplained radar traces, the document that, I take it, you reviewed is a document that consisted not only of the seven pages, but also included within it an analysis of each and every one of the alleged air-space violations; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't specifically recall that, but that's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I'm trying to figure out a way of doing this which will make everybody's life easier and not harder. And I suppose what we should do just for the moment is if we could have 65 ter 6076 up on the screen in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't know if you have it up -- I don't know whether you have it available on the screen yet or not, Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have something now in Serbo-Croat language or one of the local languages. Okay, I have now both.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. The document as it was presented to you by Ms. Bolton and which forms the basis of the plaintiff's exhibit is the next seven pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. I think my friends has stated facts that aren't yet in evidence. He said he has had the opportunity to review it before came to court, but he didn't say that it was during proofing with myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I didn't ask him whether he did or not. It's of no relevance to me whether that's occurred or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Well, you just suggested that that is when it had occurred, and, therefore, you've included in your question facts that are not in evidence. The document as it was presented to you by Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that was the document that was presented to you here in court.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I misunderstood. I thought you were talking about proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: For me, Mr. Guy-Smith, I still have P2485 on my screen, I don't have 65 ter 6076 on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I can't do much about that. That's outside of my bailiwick. If I might, I have a resolution to this, which is considering that it probably will go considerable quicker if we have the hard-copy of the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I'm told this is one in the same document, anyway, 6076 and P2485. The other one was a B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. May I just -- I am noting the time, and I'm thinking that by virtue of the fact of the electronic difficulties that we have been having, just in terms of getting things up on the screen, it may be easier because I'm not going to get through these pages in this period of time. And if I can get these pages to Mr. Sacirbey in hard-copy, we can probably get through it much quicker, since we've got, I think, about 2 minutes left or 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you suggesting we adjourn?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am. I think that's probably the sensible thing to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Well then, obviously, there's no way we can continue with Mr. Sacirbey tomorrow. And would I imagine that Mr. Sacirbey will be advised of the next time he can come back to the witness-stand. I don't think it's something that we can arrange now. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have some suggested dates. Our first priority would be Tuesday, the 7th of July. Our second priority would be the Friday -- I'm sorry, let me just consult with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, one of our --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your second priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: One of our concerns is how much longer the cross-examination will go. That will assist us in terms of selecting a date, because we have to arrange Mr. Sacirbey's evidence around the testimony of other witnesses, and that's what I have to manage at this point, so if I could get an indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate the question asked and the concern. And I wish that I could accommodate Mr. Harmon. But apart from dealing with Mr. Sacirbey's testimony, there has been, in my estimation, a legal issue that has arisen with regard to his assertion under Rule 90. And the propriety of allowing him not to answer the questions where there is an available remedy. And we are in the process of finishing the research.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's outside his testimony, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, no, but what I'm getting at is we are in the process of researching and finalising an interlocutory appeal with regard to that particular issue. So to the extent that the Appeals Chamber will be considering this particular issue, it may well affect the length of my examination, because if in fact the Appeals Chamber agrees with my position, then obviously it puts the issue of his assertion and the ruling in a different light and would necessarily change the length of my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think if you are able to estimate the balance of your cross-examination putting aside the 90E appeal, it would be very helpful, because I imagine that if on appeal you are successful and you want to put back those questions him, then we'll have to arrange another day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that. I'm trying to figure out a way of doing to both accommodate the Prosecution as well as Mr. Sacirbey, so we are not bouncing back and forth in the cyber-world of video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't know how long that appeal is going to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So that becomes difficult for to you figure into the equation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's true. Well, I wanted to alert -- I thought in all fairness to all the parties as well as to the Chamber with regard to the issue of scheduling, that that would be something of consideration. It may not be to Mr. Harmon or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's very difficult because we don't have control over the AC.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. Well, then, I think it would be fair to say that I would be taking at least two more sessions with Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You hear that, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour, and that gives me some enlightenment, and let me just consult with my colleague for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are -- we would suggest that Monday the 13th of July as our first priority in light of the information we have just received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You are aware that on both those days we are scheduled to sit in the morning, and you will sort out the change of times with --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's obviously a complicating factor, because I don't want Mr. Sacirbey to be in the room at 3 a.m. in the morning, so if there's no possibility that we can sit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting there's no possibility. You can always negotiate with the people who deal with court scheduling. But I'm saying I leave it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. I'll accept that challenge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. It's a very minor challenge. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge Picard indicates that the 13th would be better because on the 7th she is sitting also in Stanisic that day, and there may be a clash because Stanisic sits in the afternoon also. So if you shift us to the afternoon, then she literally has to ... So will you go to the 13th?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We agree, Your Honour. The 13th is our preference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. But it was your second choice?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, but it's our choice at this point because of other considerations as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Would that be okay for the Defence, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. I'm sure I can work with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith -- my apologies. Mr. Sacirbey, the plan is to postpone to the 13th of July. Would that suit you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honour, I'm glad someone finally asked me because, obviously, I have a personal/professional life, as well as some legal issues to deal with, And I thank you for the consideration. I'd like to be able to consult with my counsel, and of course Mr. Guy-Smith has raised another issue here which comes back in a much more direct fashion where my counsel may be very important. So if I may just have a day or two to consult with counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can consult with counsel. Which issue was raised by Mr. Guy-Smith, the 90E issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That's correct. And there may be others for all we know, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yea, you can consult about that. I'm just asking you about your availability to come to court, sir, as a witness. And I don't think you need counsel for that. The idea is to postpone to the 13th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honour, I did have other plans. I will change those plans because I consider the Court to deserve my full testimony and the cross-examination. And I have great respect for you and the Court that has been established there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Court appreciates your preparedness to change your schedule to accommodate the Court, it's very much appreciated. Thank you so much. Then in that event you would be required to come back to court on July the 13th, same time as today, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. Of course when I say come back to court, I mean to be where you are right now, okay. For now you are excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: For now you are excused. Once again the warning is there. You are not supposed to discuss the case with anybody during the period that you are not in court for as long as you are still in the witness-stand. Okay. See you on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I appreciate it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are excused. You may be excused. You can switch off, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. We adjourn to tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My understanding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Everybody, please sit down. I was asking, we are adjourned to tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we please sit down. It's your understanding that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's a morning sitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Tomorrow's sitting. Certainly, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is a morning sitting. I was going to say that -- [overlapping speakers]... before people stood up. Then the matter stands adjourned to tomorrow, 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom I. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: See you then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 2nd day of July, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
